procedures.title: Colonoscopy
procedures.summary: A colonoscopy is a test that looks at the inside of your whole large bowel using a thin, flexible tube with a camera. It is usually done as a day procedure with sedation.

sections.heading: What a colonoscopy is
body: A colonoscopy is an examination of the inside of your large bowel (the colon and rectum) using a long, thin, flexible tube called a colonoscope. The tube has a small camera and a light, and it is passed gently through your anus. The pictures are shown on a screen.

The colonoscopist can look at the whole lining of the bowel, take small tissue samples (biopsies) and remove growths called polyps. Polyps are common and most are harmless, but some can slowly turn into cancer over many years. Removing them is one way colonoscopy helps prevent bowel cancer.

The test is usually done with sedation or a light general anaesthetic, so most people are comfortable and remember little or nothing about it. It usually takes about 20 to 40 minutes, although you should expect to be at the hospital or day surgery unit for a few hours in total.

sections.heading: Why it may be recommended
body: There are three main reasons a colonoscopy is recommended:
bullets: Screening, when you have no symptoms but want to check for polyps or early cancer.
Investigation of symptoms such as bleeding from the bowel, a change in bowel habit, anaemia, or unexplained tummy pain.
Surveillance, when you have had polyps or bowel cancer before, or have a family history or a genetic condition that raises your risk. Your surgeon will advise how often this should be repeated.

sections.heading: Screening in Australia
body: Australia has a free National Bowel Cancer Screening Program. A simple test kit is posted to eligible people so they can collect tiny samples at home and mail them back. The test looks for invisible traces of blood in the stool. It is not a colonoscopy.

From 1 July 2024, people aged 45 to 49 can also join the program and request a free kit. Everyone aged 45 to 74 can ask their doctor about getting a kit. If a screening test is positive, it does not mean you have cancer, but you will usually be referred for a colonoscopy to find the cause.
If you have symptoms, do not wait for a screening kit. See your doctor, because symptoms need to be investigated promptly whatever your age.

sections.heading: Bowel preparation
body: The bowel preparation is the part people find hardest, but it is also the part that matters most. Your bowel needs to be completely empty so the lining can be seen clearly. If stool is left behind, polyps can be missed, the test can take longer, and the whole procedure may need to be repeated or rescheduled.
You will be given written instructions that are specific to you. In general, preparation involves:
bullets: A low-fibre diet for one or two days beforehand. This usually means white bread, white rice or pasta, plain chicken or fish, clear soup and no fruit, vegetables, seeds, nuts or wholegrains.
Clear fluids only for a period before the test. Clear fluids include water, clear broth, black tea or coffee, and clear apple juice. Avoid milk and anything cloudy, red or purple.

A strong laxative (the purgative) that you drink in one or two doses, often in the afternoon or evening before the test and again on the morning of the test. Your instructions will give the exact times.

You will need to stay close to a toilet once the laxative starts working. Diarrhoea usually begins a few hours after the first dose, and the bowel motions become clearer and more watery as the bowel empties.

sections.heading: Making the prep easier
body: Chill the laxative drink, sip it steadily rather than in large gulps, and keep clear fluids up so you do not become dehydrated. Have soft toilet paper and a barrier cream ready. Follow the timing exactly and do not skip a dose, even if the diarrhoea seems heavy, because the timing is designed around your procedure time.

Tell the clinic before the prep if you have kidney or heart problems, diabetes, or take insulin or other regular medicines. Some medicines, including blood thinners and iron tablets, may need to be adjusted. Do not stop any medicine unless you have been told to.

sections.heading: During the procedure
body: You will change into a hospital gown and lie on your left side. A small tube (a cannula) is placed in a vein in your arm for sedation. The sedation is usually given through this line. Some people have a deeper general anaesthetic instead, and your anaesthetist will discuss this with you.

The colonoscopist passes the colonoscope through your anus and gently guides it around the bowel. Air or carbon dioxide is used to open the bowel so the lining can be seen. Most people feel nothing during the test, or have only mild bloating and cramping afterwards.
Polyps found during the test are usually removed straight away using tools that pass down the colonoscope. This is called a polypectomy. Small samples of tissue may also be taken for testing.

sections.heading: Afterwards and getting home
body: You will rest in a recovery area while the sedation wears off. You may feel bloated, windy or mildly cramped, and this usually settles within a short time. You can usually eat and drink normally once you are awake.
The sedation affects your judgement, coordination and reaction times for about 24 hours. For that reason:
bullets: You must not drive for 24 hours after sedation.
You need someone to collect you and take you home. You should not take a taxi or rideshare alone.
It is best to have someone stay with you overnight.
Do not sign legal documents, make major decisions, operate machinery, or drink alcohol for 24 hours.
Plan to rest for the remainder of the day. Most people return to normal activities the next day.

sections.heading: Results and follow-up
body: The colonoscopist will usually speak with you or your support person before you go home, and you will be given a written report. If biopsies or polyps were removed, the laboratory results take about one to two weeks.

You will be told what was found, whether you need any further tests, and when your next colonoscopy should be. This interval is based on what was found and on your personal risk. If you have not heard within a few weeks, it is reasonable to phone the rooms.
If you have a polyp removed, the recommendation for your next test may be sooner than you expect. This is normal and is about checking the bowel is settling well, not a sign that something is wrong.

sections.heading: A note about private and public care
body: A colonoscopy can be done in a public hospital, or as a private patient in a private hospital or day surgery unit. In Australia, Medicare covers part of the cost of specialist care, and private health insurance may cover more. Waiting times and out-of-pocket costs differ between public and private. The rooms can explain the options and costs for your situation.

expect: Day procedure for most people
The bowel prep is the hardest part
Usually 20 to 40 minutes of examination
No driving for 24 hours after sedation
Arrange for someone to take you home

risks.name: Bleeding
risks.detail: Bleeding can occur, especially if polyps are removed. It is uncommon, and may happen during the procedure or up to a couple of weeks afterwards. Seek urgent care if you pass a lot of blood or feel unwell.

risks.name: Perforation (a tear in the bowel wall)
risks.detail: A small tear in the bowel wall is rare but serious. It may need treatment with antibiotics, a procedure to seal it, or an operation. Contact the hospital or your surgeon urgently if you develop severe pain, a hard or swollen tummy, fever or feeling very unwell.

risks.name: Reaction to sedation or anaesthetic
risks.detail: Reactions to the medicines used are uncommon. Your anaesthetist or sedation doctor will review your health and medicines beforehand to reduce the risk.

risks.name: Incomplete examination
risks.detail: Sometimes the whole bowel cannot be seen, for example if the prep was not complete, or because of narrowing, adhesions or an unusual bowel shape. Your colonoscopist will explain what was seen and whether another test is needed.

risks.name: A polyp or cancer may be missed
risks.detail: No test is perfect. A good bowel prep, an experienced colonoscopist and careful examination time all reduce the chance of missing something. This is another reason regular follow-up matters.

risks.name: Bowel preparation side effects
risks.detail: Nausea, vomiting, bloating, tummy cramps and sore skin around the bottom are common during the prep. Drinking clear fluids steadily helps. Contact the clinic if you cannot keep fluids down or feel faint.

questions.q: Will I be asleep?
questions.a: Most people have sedation, which makes you relaxed and drowsy so you are comfortable and remember little. Some people have a light general anaesthetic instead. Your surgeon and anaesthetist will discuss which is best for you.

questions.q: Do I really have to drink all of the prep?
questions.a: Yes, if you possibly can. The prep is what allows your bowel to be seen clearly. If it is not finished, polyps can be missed and the test may need to be repeated or rescheduled. If you are struggling, phone the clinic for advice rather than stopping on your own.

questions.q: Will it hurt?
questions.a: The test itself is not usually painful because of the sedation. The prep can cause tummy cramps, and afterwards you may feel bloated or windy for a short time. Tell the staff if you are uncomfortable, as they can adjust your sedation.

questions.q: When can I drive and go back to work?
questions.a: You must not drive for 24 hours after sedation. Most people can return to normal activities, including work, the next day. If you had polyps removed you may be advised to take it a little easier.

questions.q: When will I know the results?
questions.a: You will usually be told what was seen before you go home, and you will be given a written report. Results from biopsies or removed polyps take about one to two weeks. You will also be told when your next colonoscopy is due.

questions.q: Can I still take my regular medicines?
questions.a: Most medicines can continue, but some such as blood thinners, diabetes medicines and iron may need to be adjusted. Tell the clinic about everything you take, including supplements, before you start the prep.

procedures.disclaimer: This is general information only. Every person's situation is different, and Dr Sutherland will discuss your individual circumstances, the reasons for your procedure and your particular risks with you.

procedures.title: Colon resection (colectomy)
procedures.summary: A colon resection removes the part of the large bowel containing a tumour or diseased segment, then rejoins the healthy ends. Most people do not need a stoma.

sections.heading: What the operation involves
body: A colon resection, also called a colectomy or bowel resection, is an operation to remove a segment of the large bowel. It is most often done for bowel cancer, and sometimes for other conditions such as diverticular disease, Crohn disease or a narrowed or blocked segment.

The surgeon removes the diseased section along with a margin of normal bowel on each side, so the remaining bowel is healthy. The two ends are then joined back together. This join is called an anastomosis. The operation is done under a general anaesthetic.

The name of the operation depends on which part is removed. Removing the right side is a right hemicolectomy, the left side is a left hemicolectomy, the sigmoid colon is a sigmoid colectomy, and the middle section is a transverse colectomy. Your surgeon will explain the exact plan for you.

sections.heading: Lymph nodes
body: When the operation is for cancer, the surgeon also removes the lymph nodes and fatty tissue connected to that section of bowel. Lymph nodes are small glands that filter fluid, and they are one of the first places bowel cancer can spread to.

The nodes are examined under a microscope by a pathologist. This helps show how far the cancer has spread and whether you might benefit from chemotherapy afterwards. Removing the nodes is an important part of the cancer operation and is done at the same time as the bowel is removed.

sections.heading: Will I need a stoma?
body: Most people who have a colon resection do not need a stoma. The bowel is usually joined back together and you continue to pass stool normally through the anus.

If the join is not safe, or the bowel is very blocked or inflamed, the surgeon may decide during the operation to bring one end of the bowel out onto the skin of the tummy. This is a stoma, and waste is collected in a bag worn over it. This is much more common with rectal surgery than with colon surgery.

If a stoma is needed, it may be temporary while the bowel heals, with a second smaller operation later to reverse it. A specialist stoma care nurse will teach you how to care for it and will support you. A stoma is not something you have to manage on your own. Your surgeon will discuss the possibility with you before the operation.

sections.heading: Enhanced recovery and your hospital stay
body: Many bowel operations now follow an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) program. This is a planned approach to your care before, during and after the operation. It includes clear information before admission, avoiding long fasting, special carbohydrate drinks before surgery, tailored anaesthetic and pain relief, and getting you eating, drinking and walking as soon as it is safe.

Enhanced recovery is well established for colorectal surgery. It helps reduce complications and shorten the time spent in hospital. You are an important part of the program, and the ward staff and dietitian will guide you day by day.
The length of stay varies with the operation and your general health. Many people go home within a few days. There is more detail on a separate page about enhanced recovery after colorectal surgery.

sections.heading: Eating and drinking afterwards
body: You will usually be able to drink soon after the operation and start eating soft food within a day or so, as your bowel wakes up. You may be advised to follow a lower fibre diet for a few weeks while the join heals. A dietitian will see you in hospital.

As things settle, you can reintroduce foods one at a time, starting with small amounts, so you can tell what suits you. Some people notice loose motions or constipation for a while. This usually settles, but tell your surgeon if it persists.
Drink plenty of fluid, especially water. Very hard stools are best avoided in the weeks after surgery.

sections.heading: Recovery timeline
body: You may feel tired and a little sore for the first week or two. Pain is usually managed with tablets, and it is important to keep moving gently.

Avoid heavy lifting, straining and strenuous exercise for about six weeks while the abdominal wall and the bowel join heal. Walking is encouraged from early on. Driving can usually resume once you are comfortable and able to react normally, often around two weeks, but this varies and you should check with your surgeon.
Most people feel substantially better within four to six weeks, but full recovery can take a few months. Energy levels often improve gradually rather than all at once.

sections.heading: What happens after surgery
body: The removed bowel and lymph nodes go to a laboratory for examination. The results help your team decide whether further treatment such as chemotherapy is recommended. Your case is often discussed at a multidisciplinary team meeting, where surgeons, cancer doctors, radiologists and pathologists plan care together.

You will be given a follow-up appointment to discuss the results and any further treatment. Follow-up usually continues for several years with check-ups, blood tests and scans or colonoscopies at intervals.

expect: Removes the diseased segment of bowel
Usually rejoined, no stoma needed
Lymph nodes removed for cancer
Often home within a few days
Full recovery may take months

risks.name: Anastomotic leak
risks.detail: The join in the bowel can occasionally leak. This is uncommon but serious. It may cause pain, fever and feeling unwell, and may need antibiotics, a drain, or further surgery. It is one of the main reasons a surgeon sometimes creates a stoma to protect the join.

risks.name: Bleeding
risks.detail: Bleeding can occur during or after the operation. It usually settles by itself, but occasionally a blood transfusion or a further procedure is needed.

risks.name: Infection
risks.detail: Wound or abdominal infection can occur. It is usually treated with antibiotics and sometimes by draining a collection of fluid. Antibiotics are often given around the time of surgery to reduce this risk.

risks.name: Ileus (the bowel is slow to wake up)
risks.detail: After abdominal surgery the bowel can be sluggish for a few days, causing nausea, bloating and wind. This usually settles with time, fluids and gentle movement. If it does not, a tube may be passed through the nose into the stomach to relieve it.

risks.name: Blood clots in the legs or lungs
risks.detail: Clots are a risk after any major operation. You will be given support stockings, compression devices and often blood-thinning medicine, and you will be encouraged to move early. Tell staff straight away about calf pain, breathlessness or chest pain.

risks.name: Damage to nearby structures
risks.detail: In rare cases, other organs such as the ureter (the tube from the kidney to the bladder), the spleen or nearby bowel can be injured and need repair. Your surgeon will explain if this is a particular risk for you.

risks.name: Death
risks.detail: Serious complications leading to death are rare, but they can happen after major bowel surgery. This is why your team assesses your general health and heart and lung fitness carefully before the operation.

risks.name: Change in bowel habit
risks.detail: Bowel habits can change after a section of bowel is removed. Some people have looser or more frequent motions, others become constipated. This often settles over weeks to months. Diet, fluid and sometimes medicine can help.

questions.q: Will I need a stoma appliance?
questions.a: Most people having a colon resection do not need a stoma. The bowel is usually joined back together. Your surgeon will tell you before the operation if a stoma is likely, and whether it would be temporary or permanent.

questions.q: How long will I be in hospital?
questions.a: This varies with the operation and how you recover. Many people go home within a few days with an enhanced recovery program. Your surgeon will give you a more specific estimate.

questions.q: Will the cancer come back?
questions.a: Nobody can promise an outcome. Surgery removes the cancer that can be seen and the surrounding lymph nodes, and further treatment such as chemotherapy may be advised. Your team will discuss your individual situation and follow-up plan with you.

questions.q: When can I eat normally and go back to work?
questions.a: You usually start with fluids and soft food within a day or so, then build up. Many people return to lighter duties within four to six weeks, and to heavier work later. Avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks.

questions.q: Will I need chemotherapy?
questions.a: This depends on the stage of the cancer and the lymph node results. Your case will be discussed by a multidisciplinary team, and the recommendation will be explained to you at follow-up.

questions.q: Where is the surgery done, and what will it cost?
questions.a: It can be done in a public or private hospital in Australia. Medicare covers part of specialist care and private health insurance may cover more, but out-of-pocket costs differ. The rooms can explain the options and costs for your situation.

procedures.title: Laparoscopic colon resection
procedures.summary: Keyhole bowel surgery removes a section of colon through several small cuts instead of one large one. Recovery is often quicker, but your surgeon will advise whether it suits you.

sections.heading: What keyhole surgery means
body: Laparoscopic surgery, often called keyhole surgery, is a way of doing the same bowel operation through much smaller openings. Instead of one long incision, the surgeon makes several small cuts, usually about one to two centimetres each, and one slightly larger opening so the removed section of bowel can be taken out.

The operation inside is the same operation. The same section of bowel is removed, the same lymph nodes are taken when cancer is being treated, and the bowel is joined back together in the same way. The difference is how the surgeon reaches the area and how much of the abdominal wall is opened.
Keyhole surgery is done under a general anaesthetic. Your surgeon will explain the plan, and whether keyhole or open surgery is more appropriate for you.

sections.heading: How it is done
body: A small tube is placed through one of the cuts, and carbon dioxide gas is used to gently inflate the abdomen. This creates room to see and work. The gas is removed at the end of the operation, and any remaining gas passes naturally.

A thin camera with a light is passed through one of the tubes, giving a magnified view on a screen in the operating theatre. The surgeon uses long, fine instruments passed through the other openings. The section of bowel is freed, its blood supply is carefully controlled, and it is brought out through the slightly larger opening.
The bowel is then rejoined, and the small cuts are closed. The slightly larger opening is usually a few centimetres long and may sit in a natural skin crease.

sections.heading: Possible advantages
body: When keyhole surgery goes well, many people experience:
bullets: Smaller scars and less wound discomfort.
Less pain in the first days after surgery, which can mean less need for strong painkillers.
A shorter stay in hospital for many people.
A faster return to walking, eating and everyday activities.
A lower risk of some wound problems such as infection or hernia.

sections.heading: Being realistic about it
body: These advantages are common but they are not guaranteed. Recovery depends on your general health, the reason for the operation, how the surgery goes, and how your bowel behaves afterwards. Some people recover just as quickly after open surgery, and some keyhole operations need to be converted to open surgery partway through.
No approach is better for everyone. Your surgeon will recommend the approach they believe is safest and most suitable for you, and will explain the reasons.

sections.heading: When open surgery may be needed
body: Sometimes open surgery through a longer incision is safer or more practical. This may be because:
bullets: The tumour is large, or it is stuck to other structures.
There is scarring from previous operations or infection inside the abdomen.
The bowel is very blocked or has perforated, and the operation needs to be done quickly.
There has been bleeding during the operation, or the view is not clear enough.
Your general health, heart or lung condition makes a shorter operation safer.
The surgeon is not able to complete the operation safely using keyhole techniques.

sections.heading: If a conversion happens
body: A conversion to open surgery is not a failure and is not usually caused by anything you did. It is a safety decision made by your surgeon during the operation, based on what they find. It may mean a longer incision, a longer stay and a slower recovery, but the operation itself is completed.
Your surgeon will explain what happened and why, and will adjust your recovery plan accordingly.

sections.heading: Recovery
body: You will be encouraged to get up and move around soon after surgery, usually the same day or the next day. This helps your circulation, your breathing and your bowel. You will start drinking and eating as your bowel wakes up.

The small cuts usually heal well. You may feel some shoulder-tip discomfort for a day or two from the gas used during the operation. Avoid heavy lifting and straining for about six weeks. Many people return to lighter activities within two to four weeks, but this varies and your surgeon will guide you.

expect: Several small cuts, one slightly larger
Same operation internally as open surgery
Often less pain and shorter stay
Open surgery may still be needed
Avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks

risks.name: The same risks as open surgery
risks.detail: Keyhole surgery does not remove the risks of bowel surgery. Anastomotic leak, bleeding, infection, ileus, blood clots and, rarely, death can still occur. Your surgeon will discuss these with you.

risks.name: Conversion to open surgery
risks.detail: The operation may need to be completed through a larger incision. This is a safety decision made during surgery and may mean a longer stay and slower recovery.

risks.name: Injury from the instruments or gas
risks.detail: Uncommon problems can include injury to bowel or other organs from an instrument, or effects from the carbon dioxide gas. These are usually recognised and managed during or after the operation.

risks.name: Wound problems at the larger opening
risks.detail: The slightly larger opening used to remove the bowel can become infected, or later develop a hernia. Keeping the wound clean and avoiding heavy lifting while it heals reduces this risk.

questions.q: Is keyhole surgery better than open surgery?
questions.a: For many people it offers smaller scars, less pain and a quicker recovery. But it is not suitable for everyone, and some operations are safer done through an open incision. Your surgeon will recommend the approach best suited to you.

questions.q: How big are the scars?
questions.a: Most cuts are about one to two centimetres. The opening used to remove the bowel is usually a few centimetres long. Scars fade over months.

questions.q: Will the cancer be removed as thoroughly?
questions.a: Yes. The operation inside is the same, including removal of the lymph nodes. The aim of cancer surgery is not changed by using keyhole techniques.

questions.q: What happens if you have to switch to open surgery?
questions.a: Your surgeon will make that decision during the operation if it is safer. It is not a failure, and the operation is still completed. It may mean a longer incision and a slower recovery.

questions.q: How long until I am back to normal?
questions.a: Many people are walking and eating within a day or two and back to lighter activities within two to four weeks. Full recovery, including heavy lifting, usually takes about six weeks or more.

procedures.title: Enhanced recovery after surgery
procedures.summary: Enhanced recovery is a planned approach that helps you get ready for bowel surgery and recover faster afterwards. It is well established and can shorten your hospital stay.

sections.heading: What enhanced recovery is
body: Enhanced recovery after surgery, often called ERAS, is a structured program of care for people having major operations, including bowel surgery. It brings together the surgeon, anaesthetist, nurses, physiotherapist and dietitian so that every part of your care follows the same plan.

The aim is to prepare you well, reduce the stress of surgery on your body, and help you get back to eating, moving and normal activity safely and as soon as possible. Enhanced recovery is well established in colorectal surgery. It has been shown to improve recovery and shorten the time people spend in hospital.
You are not a passive patient in this program. Your active involvement is one of the most important parts of it.

sections.heading: Before your operation
body: You will be given clear information about what to expect, often at a pre-admission clinic. This includes what the operation involves, how your pain will be managed, what you will be asked to do afterwards, and who to contact with questions. Being well informed helps reduce anxiety and helps you plan.

You may also have blood tests, heart and lung checks, and a review of your medicines. If you smoke, stopping before surgery helps healing and reduces complications. If you can, build up some gentle exercise and good nutrition beforehand.

Where possible, you will not fast for a long time before surgery. You may be given a carbohydrate drink a couple of hours before the operation. This helps keep your body fuelled and can reduce the stress response to surgery.
Most bowel resections no longer need a full bowel preparation. This is a change from the past. Your surgeon will tell you if a prep is needed for your particular operation.
Some people are given medicine before surgery to help with comfort afterwards, and antibiotics are usually given around the time of the operation.

sections.heading: During your operation
body: Your anaesthetist tailors the anaesthetic and pain relief to you. This can include regional or local anaesthetic blocks, which numb the area and reduce the need for stronger painkillers afterwards.

Where possible, keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery is used, because it usually means smaller wounds and less pain. Drains and nasogastric tubes are avoided when they are not needed. A nasogastric tube is a thin tube passed through the nose into the stomach. It is only used if there is a specific reason.
Fluids given through a drip are carefully matched to what your body needs. Too much fluid can slow the return of normal bowel function.

sections.heading: After your operation
body: The days after surgery follow a clear plan:
bullets: Pain relief uses a combination of medicines, aiming to avoid relying heavily on strong opioid painkillers such as morphine. Opioids can make the bowel sluggish, so using other medicines alongside them helps you recover.
You will be helped out of bed and encouraged to walk on the day of surgery or the next day. Getting moving helps your lungs, your circulation and your bowel.
You will start sipping fluids soon after surgery and build up to soft food and then normal food as you feel able. You do not need to wait for your bowel to fully wake up before eating.
You will be encouraged to chew gum or drink peppermint tea if your team suggests it, as these can help the bowel start working again.
Your drip and any tubes are removed as soon as they are no longer needed.
You will be given support stockings and often blood-thinning medicine to reduce the risk of clots.

sections.heading: Your part in it
body: The things you do make a real difference. Try to:
bullets: Ask questions and make sure you understand the plan before the operation.
Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and medicines.
Sit up, take deep breaths and use your breathing device if given one.
Get up and walk as soon as the staff say it is safe, and keep walking regularly.
Tell the staff about your pain, nausea or any worries rather than waiting.
Eat and drink as advised, even if your appetite is small at first.
Have a support person who can help you at home and bring you in.

sections.heading: Getting home and afterwards
body: You will go home when you are eating and drinking, your pain is controlled with tablets, and you are moving safely. You will be given clear instructions about medicines, wound care, diet, activity and who to call if something worries you.

Keep walking at home, build up gradually, and avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks or as advised. Keep your follow-up appointments. If you develop fever, severe pain, vomiting, a wound that looks infected, or you cannot pass urine or open your bowels, contact your surgeon or the hospital.

expect: Starts before your operation
You eat and walk early afterwards
Pain relief that limits strong opioids
Avoids drains and tubes where possible
Shown to shorten hospital stay

risks.name: The operation still carries risk
risks.detail: Enhanced recovery improves recovery but does not remove the risks of bowel surgery, such as anastomotic leak, bleeding, infection, clots and, rarely, death. Your surgeon will discuss these with you.

risks.name: Nausea or vomiting early on
risks.detail: Some people feel sick when they start eating again, and may need anti-nausea medicine or a slower build-up of food. This is usually temporary.

risks.name: Feeling faint or dizzy when you first get up
risks.detail: Getting up early can cause a brief drop in blood pressure. Staff will help you the first few times to keep you safe.

risks.name: The plan may need to change
risks.detail: If you develop a complication, your team may slow parts of the program or add treatments. This is a normal part of safe care and not a failure of the plan.

questions.q: Do I have to do a bowel prep?
questions.a: For most bowel resections, a full bowel prep is no longer needed. Your surgeon will tell you if your operation is one of the exceptions.

questions.q: Why am I given a sugary drink before surgery?
questions.a: A carbohydrate drink a couple of hours before the operation helps keep your body fuelled and reduces the stress of surgery. It is part of avoiding a long fast.

questions.q: Will I be in pain?
questions.a: You will have some discomfort, but the plan uses a mix of pain medicines, including local anaesthetic blocks, to keep it manageable while avoiding heavy reliance on strong opioids.

questions.q: What if I cannot eat after surgery?
questions.a: You start with small amounts of fluid and build up. If you feel sick, the staff can adjust your medicines and the pace. A dietitian is available if needed.

questions.q: Does this mean I go home sooner?
questions.a: Enhanced recovery has been shown to shorten hospital stays and improve recovery for many people having bowel surgery. How soon you go home still depends on how you personally recover.

questions.q: What can my family do to help?
questions.a: Family and carers can help you understand the plan, encourage you to walk and drink, and support you at home. They are welcome to be part of the discussions.

procedures.title: Rectal resection
procedures.summary: A rectal resection removes part of the rectum containing a tumour and rejoins the bowel. It is more complex than colon surgery and may involve a temporary stoma.

sections.heading: How rectal surgery differs from colon surgery
body: The rectum is the last part of the large bowel, sitting deep in the pelvis just above the anus. Operations on the rectum are different from operations further up the colon in several important ways.

The rectum sits close to the pelvic nerves that control bladder, bowel and sexual function, and close to the muscles of the anus that control continence. The space is narrow and deep, which makes the operation technically more demanding. Rectal cancer can also behave differently from colon cancer, and treatment often includes chemotherapy or radiotherapy before surgery.
Because of this, rectal surgery is usually done by a surgeon with specific training in colorectal surgery, and the planning involves imaging and often discussion at a multidisciplinary team meeting.

sections.heading: Staging with MRI and other tests
body: Before surgery you will have tests to show exactly where the tumour is and how far it has grown. These are used to plan the operation and to decide whether treatment before surgery is needed.

An MRI scan of the pelvis is particularly important for rectal cancer. It shows how close the tumour is to the surrounding tissue and the mesorectum, the fatty tissue around the rectum that contains lymph nodes. This helps the surgeon plan a safe margin of normal tissue around the tumour.

You may also have a CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, blood tests, and sometimes a PET scan. A colonoscopy is done to look at the rest of the bowel. Your team will explain what each test is for.

sections.heading: Treatment before surgery
body: Some rectal cancers are treated with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or both before the operation. This is called neoadjuvant treatment. It aims to shrink the tumour, make it easier to remove, and reduce the risk of the cancer returning in the pelvis.

Not everyone needs this. The decision depends on the stage and position of the tumour and on the MRI findings. Your case will be discussed by a team of specialists, and the recommended plan will be explained to you before anything starts.

sections.heading: Total mesorectal excision
body: For most rectal cancers, the operation includes a technique called total mesorectal excision, or TME. The mesorectum is the package of fatty tissue and lymph nodes that surrounds the rectum and carries its blood supply.

In TME, the surgeon removes the rectum together with this whole fatty package, carefully keeping its outer surface intact. This is important because cancer can spread into these lymph nodes, and leaving the package undisturbed reduces the chance of cancer being left behind or seeding into the pelvis.
TME is a precise operation that needs care around the pelvic nerves. It is the standard approach for rectal cancer and is one reason outcomes for rectal cancer have improved.

sections.heading: Low anterior resection
body: The most common operation for upper and middle rectal cancers is a low anterior resection. The surgeon removes the diseased part of the rectum and joins the remaining rectum or colon down to the anus. This join is called an anastomosis.
The lower the join sits in the pelvis, the more careful the surgeon must be about its blood supply and tension, and about protecting it while it heals.

sections.heading: Temporary ileostomy
body: When the join is very low, the surgeon may bring a loop of the small bowel out onto the skin of the tummy to divert the stool away from the join while it heals. This is called a loop ileostomy. It is usually temporary.

The ileostomy is generally reversed in a second, smaller operation some weeks or months later, once the join has healed and any further treatment such as chemotherapy is finished. Not everyone needs an ileostomy, and your surgeon will discuss the likelihood with you before your operation.
A specialist stoma care nurse will show you how to look after the stoma and the stoma before you go home. Many people find this is easier to manage than they expected.

sections.heading: Bowel function after a low rectal resection
body: The rectum acts as a reservoir, storing stool until it is convenient to go to the toilet. When part or all of the rectum is removed, this storage function is reduced. This can lead to changes in bowel habit known as low anterior resection syndrome, or LARS.
Features can include:
bullets: Going to the toilet more often, sometimes many times a day.
Urgency, where you need to go suddenly and cannot wait long.
Clustering, where you pass several motions over a short period.
Difficulty telling wind from stool, and occasional leakage.
A feeling of not completely emptying.

sections.heading: Living with LARS
body: These symptoms can be distressing and can affect work and social life. It is important to know that they often improve over time. Many people notice gradual improvement over 12 to 24 months as the bowel adapts.

There is help available. Your surgeon or a continence nurse can discuss diet changes, fibre and fluid adjustments, medicines that slow the bowel, pelvic floor exercises, and sometimes sacral nerve stimulation. If bowel function is affecting your life, tell your team. It is a common problem and there is no need to manage it alone.

sections.heading: Recovery
body: You will usually be in hospital for several days, following an enhanced recovery plan. You will be helped to eat and walk early. If you have an ileostomy, the stoma nurse will work with you before discharge.

Recovery takes time. Many people feel tired for several weeks, and bowel function continues to change for months. Avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks. Follow-up will include regular check-ups and tests, sometimes for several years.

expect: Removes part of the rectum and rejoins bowel
MRI is used to plan the operation
A temporary ileostomy is sometimes needed
Bowel habit changes are common at first
Function often improves over 12 to 24 months

risks.name: Anastomotic leak
risks.detail: The join in the bowel can leak. This risk is higher with low rectal joins, which is one reason a temporary ileostomy is sometimes used to protect the join. A leak may need antibiotics, a drain or further surgery.

risks.name: Low anterior resection syndrome (LARS)
risks.detail: Frequency, urgency, clustering and occasional leakage are common after low rectal surgery. Symptoms often improve over 12 to 24 months but can persist. Treatments and support are available.

risks.name: Bleeding or infection
risks.detail: Bleeding around the operation and infection in the wound or pelvis can occur. These are usually managed with antibiotics, drainage or occasionally further treatment.

risks.name: Damage to pelvic nerves
risks.detail: Nerves controlling bladder, bowel and sexual function sit close to the rectum. The surgeon takes great care to protect them, but in some operations function can be affected. Your surgeon will discuss this risk with you.

risks.name: Stoma complications
risks.detail: If an ileostomy is formed, problems such as skin irritation, blockage, dehydration, or a hernia near the stoma can occur. A stoma care nurse can help manage these.

risks.name: Blood clots in the legs or lungs
risks.detail: Major pelvic surgery increases the risk of clots. Support stockings, compression devices and blood-thinning medicine are used to reduce this. Report calf pain, breathlessness or chest pain promptly.

risks.name: The cancer returning in the pelvis
risks.detail: Despite careful surgery and any treatment before or after the operation, cancer can return. This is why follow-up with regular check-ups and scans is arranged, and why further treatment may be recommended.

questions.q: Will I need a stoma?
questions.a: Some people having a low rectal resection need a temporary loop ileostomy to protect the join while it heals. It is usually reversed in a second, smaller operation. Your surgeon will tell you how likely this is in your case.

questions.q: Why do I need an MRI before surgery?
questions.a: An MRI shows how close the tumour is to the surrounding tissue and lymph nodes. It helps your surgeon plan a safe operation and decide whether treatment before surgery is needed.

questions.q: Will my bowel habit return to normal?
questions.a: It often improves, but it may not be exactly as it was before. Frequency, urgency and clustering are common at first and usually settle over 12 to 24 months. There are treatments and support if it does not.

questions.q: What is a total mesorectal excision?
questions.a: It means removing the rectum together with the fatty tissue and lymph nodes that surround it, keeping the outer surface intact. It is the standard operation for rectal cancer and helps reduce the chance of the cancer returning.

questions.q: Will I need chemotherapy or radiotherapy?
questions.a: Some rectal cancers are treated with chemotherapy, radiotherapy or both before surgery, and some people need chemotherapy afterwards. This depends on the stage and position of the tumour and is discussed by your specialist team.

questions.q: How long will I be off work?
questions.a: This varies widely. Many people need six to twelve weeks away from work, and sometimes longer if they have further treatment. Your surgeon will guide you based on your recovery and your type of work.

procedures.title: Abdominoperineal resection
procedures.summary: An APER removes the rectum and anus for very low rectal cancers, and a permanent colostomy is formed. It is a major change, and support is available.

sections.heading: What an APER is
body: An abdominoperineal resection, also called an APER or APR, is an operation for cancers very low in the rectum. It removes the rectum, the anal canal and the anus itself.

Because the anus is removed, there is no longer a way for stool to leave the body in the usual way. The surgeon brings the end of the colon out through the abdominal wall to form a permanent colostomy, and stool is collected in a bag worn over it.

The operation is done under a general anaesthetic. It is usually performed when the cancer is too close to the anal sphincter muscles to leave them behind safely, or when the sphincter cannot be preserved.

sections.heading: Why it may be recommended
body: The sphincter muscles keep you continent. If a cancer is growing into or very close to these muscles, removing the cancer completely may mean removing the muscles as well. An APER is one of the operations that can achieve this.

An APER may also be recommended if the sphincter has already been badly damaged, if continence was poor before surgery, or if an earlier attempt to preserve the sphincter is not safe or has not worked.

Your surgeon will explain why they are recommending this operation for you, and what the alternatives are. Sometimes a very low anterior resection with a coloanal join is possible instead. This depends on the exact position and stage of the cancer.

sections.heading: How the operation is done
body: There are two parts to the operation. From the abdomen, the surgeon frees the rectum and lower colon and removes the lymph nodes and fatty tissue around the rectum. This part may be done by keyhole or open surgery.

From the perineum, the surgeon removes the anus and the lower rectum through an incision around the anal opening. The perineal wound is then closed. Sometimes a mesh or tissue flap is used to help the area heal.

The end of the colon is brought through the abdominal wall to form the colostomy, usually on the left side of the tummy. Before the operation, a stoma nurse will mark a suitable spot for the stoma with you, so the stoma sits comfortably with your clothing.

sections.heading: The perineal wound
body: The wound between the buttocks, where the anus was removed, needs care while it heals. It can be sore, and it heals more slowly than a wound on the abdomen for some people.

You will be shown how to keep it clean and dry. You may be advised not to sit flat for long periods at first, and to use a cushion or a special ring if sitting is uncomfortable. Your nurse will check the wound regularly.

Tell your team if the wound becomes more painful, smells offensive, or discharges pus, or if you develop a fever. Occasionally the wound does not heal as expected and further care or a small procedure is needed.

sections.heading: Living with a colostomy
body: A colostomy is a significant change and it is normal to have mixed feelings about it. Many people worry about how it will look, whether it will smell, whether others will notice, and how it will affect work, travel, sport and intimacy.

In practice, most people find a routine that works for them. Modern bags are flat, secure and discreet, and they are emptied or changed on a schedule that suits you. The stool from a colostomy is usually more formed than from an ileostomy, because it has passed through more of the colon.

A stoma care nurse will teach you how to change and empty the stoma, care for the skin around the stoma, and manage diet and wind. You will have contact details so you can get help after you go home. Support is also available through stoma associations and bowel cancer organisations.

You can usually shower and bathe normally, and return to sport, swimming and travel. Tell your nurse about any worries, including about body image and sexual function. These are common concerns and there is help for them.

sections.heading: Recovery
body: You will usually be in hospital for several days or longer, depending on your recovery and the perineal wound. You will be encouraged to eat, drink and walk early as part of an enhanced recovery plan.
Avoid heavy lifting and straining for about six weeks or as advised. Healing of the perineal wound can take several weeks to a few months. Tiredness is common at first.
Some people have chemotherapy after the operation. Your team will discuss whether this is recommended once the pathology results are available.

sections.heading: Adjusting emotionally
body: It is completely reasonable to find the idea of a permanent stoma difficult. Losing the anus and changing how your body works is a real loss, and people grieve for it in different ways. Some people feel low or anxious before or after the operation.

You do not have to cope alone. Your stoma nurse, your surgeon, your general practitioner and a psychologist or counsellor can all help. Speaking with someone who has had the same operation can also be valuable. Ask your team if you would like to be put in touch with support.
For many people, life with a stoma becomes normal within a few months, and the relief of having the cancer treated is significant.

expect: Removes the rectum and the anus
A permanent colostomy is formed
Two wounds: abdomen and perineum
Stoma nurse support before and after
Support is available for adjustment

risks.name: Perineal wound problems
risks.detail: The wound where the anus was removed can be slow to heal, become infected, or discharge. It may need dressing care, antibiotics or, occasionally, a small procedure. This is one of the more common issues after an APER.

risks.name: Anastomotic problems and bleeding
risks.detail: Bleeding can occur during or after the operation. Because the bowel is not rejoined in an APER, the usual leak risk at a join does not apply, but other bleeding and pelvic collections can occur.

risks.name: Infection
risks.detail: Infection can affect the abdominal wound, the perineal wound or the pelvis. It is usually treated with antibiotics and sometimes drainage.

risks.name: Damage to pelvic nerves
risks.detail: Nerves controlling bladder and sexual function sit close to the rectum. The surgeon takes care to protect them, but function can occasionally be affected. Discuss any concerns with your surgeon before the operation.

risks.name: Stoma complications
risks.detail: Problems can include skin irritation, a hernia near the stoma, a stoma that narrows or prolapses, or blockage. A stoma care nurse can usually manage these, with surgery occasionally needed.

risks.name: Blood clots in the legs or lungs
risks.detail: Major pelvic surgery increases clot risk. Support stockings, compression devices and blood-thinning medicine are used. Report calf pain, breathlessness or chest pain promptly.

risks.name: Death
risks.detail: Serious complications leading to death are rare but can occur after major surgery. Your team assesses your health and fitness before the operation to reduce this risk.

questions.q: Is the colostomy permanent?
questions.a: Yes. Because the anus is removed, there is no other way for stool to leave the body. The stoma care nurse will help you learn to manage it, and most people settle into a routine.

questions.q: Will people be able to tell I have a stoma?
questions.a: Modern bags are flat and discreet, and most clothing hides them. You will be shown how to choose and fit a bag that suits your body and lifestyle.

questions.q: Can I still swim, travel and play sport?
questions.a: Yes, most people return to these activities. You can shower and bathe normally, and bags are secure. Your stoma nurse can give you tips for travel and sport.

questions.q: How long will the perineal wound take to heal?
questions.a: It varies. Some wounds heal in a few weeks, others take several months. Your nurse will check it regularly and tell you how to care for it.

questions.q: Is there someone I can talk to about how I am feeling?
questions.a: Yes. Your stoma nurse, surgeon and general practitioner can all help, and referral to a psychologist or counsellor is available. Some people also find it helpful to speak with someone who has had the same operation.

questions.q: Will I need more treatment after surgery?
questions.a: Some people have chemotherapy afterwards. This depends on the pathology results and the stage of the cancer, and will be discussed with you at follow-up.

procedures.title: Surgery for haemorrhoids
procedures.summary: Surgery removes troublesome haemorrhoids when simpler treatments have not worked. It is only needed for a minority of people, and the days afterwards can be sore.

sections.heading: What haemorrhoids are
body: Haemorrhoids, sometimes called piles, are pads of blood vessels and supporting tissue that everyone has inside the anal canal. They help with continence. They only become a problem when they enlarge or prolapse.

Symptoms include bright red bleeding, itching, a lump or tissue coming out, mucus discharge, and sometimes pain. Bleeding from the bottom should always be checked by a doctor, because it can have causes other than haemorrhoids.
External haemorrhoids sit under the skin near the anus. If a blood clot forms in one it becomes very painful and appears as a firm blue lump.

sections.heading: Grading explained simply
body: Internal haemorrhoids are graded by how far they prolapse, that is, how much they come out:
bullets: Grade 1: they do not come out.
Grade 2: they come out when you pass a stool but go back in on their own.
Grade 3: they come out and need to be pushed back in.
Grade 4: they stay out and cannot be pushed back in.

sections.heading: Treatments before surgery
body: Surgery is only needed for a minority of people with haemorrhoids. Most are helped by simpler measures, and these remain important even if you do have surgery.

The first steps are to increase fibre and fluid, avoid straining and long periods on the toilet, and not delay the urge to go. A fibre supplement and plenty of water keep the stool soft and bulky. A pharmacist can advise on creams and stool softeners.

If symptoms continue, your surgeon may recommend a procedure done in the rooms or as a day case. These include rubber band ligation, where a small band is placed at the base of the haemorrhoid so it shrinks and falls away, and other treatments such as sclerotherapy or infrared coagulation.
Rubber band ligation works for many grade 1, 2 and some grade 3 haemorrhoids. Several sessions are sometimes needed. It is usually well tolerated, though a dull ache for a day or two is common.

sections.heading: Surgery: the options
body: If simpler treatments have not worked, or the haemorrhoids are large or badly prolapsed, an operation may be recommended. The two main operations are:
bullets: Excisional haemorrhoidectomy: the haemorrhoidal tissue is cut out. This is a very effective operation for controlling symptoms, but it is the most painful of the options during recovery.
Stapled haemorrhoidopexy: the haemorrhoids are pulled back inside and stapled into place. There is usually less pain afterwards than with excision, but it is suitable only for certain haemorrhoids.
Haemorrhoidal artery ligation is another option used by some surgeons, where stitches are used to reduce the blood supply to the haemorrhoids so they shrink.

sections.heading: Choosing an operation
body: The right choice depends on the type and grade of your haemorrhoids, your symptoms, your other health conditions and your surgeon's assessment. Each operation has its own balance of effectiveness and risks.
Your surgeon will explain the options, why they recommend one for you, and what the recovery is likely to involve. Ask as many questions as you need to before deciding.

sections.heading: The first days afterwards
body: It is honest to say that haemorrhoid surgery is generally painful for the first one to two weeks, particularly after an excisional haemorrhoidectomy. The pain usually eases gradually after that. This is worth knowing in advance so you can plan.
Most people go home the same day or the following day. You will be given pain relief, which may include a combination of medicines, along with stool softeners and advice on fibre and fluids.
Warm shallow baths, called sitz baths, two or three times a day and after a bowel movement, help ease pain and keep the area clean. Pat the area dry rather than rubbing. Keep your stools soft.

Many people feel anxious about the first bowel movement after surgery. It is important, and it is usually less painful than expected. Stool softeners and fibre make it easier. Do not hold on or avoid going to the toilet.
Plan for about two to four weeks before you are back to your full level of activity. Avoid heavy lifting and straining while you heal.

sections.heading: When to seek help
body: Contact your surgeon or seek urgent care if you have heavy or non-stop bleeding, severe pain not controlled by your medicines, fever, a lot of swelling, pus-like discharge, or if you cannot pass urine. If you cannot open your bowels for several days despite softeners, tell your surgeon.

expect: Only needed for a minority of people
Day surgery or one night in hospital
Generally sore for 1 to 2 weeks
Stool softeners and sitz baths help

risks.name: Pain
risks.detail: Pain after haemorrhoid surgery is expected, especially after excisional surgery. It is usually worst in the first week or two and then eases. Pain relief, stool softeners and sitz baths help. Contact your surgeon if pain is not controlled.

risks.name: Bleeding
risks.detail: Some bleeding is common, particularly with the first bowel movement. Heavy or non-stop bleeding, or passing large clots, needs urgent medical attention.

risks.name: Infection
risks.detail: Infection at the operation site is uncommon but can occur. It is usually treated with antibiotics and wound care.

risks.name: Narrowing of the anal canal (stenosis)
risks.detail: Scarring can occasionally narrow the anal opening, making it harder to pass stool. This may need stretching or further treatment.

risks.name: Difficulty controlling wind or stool
risks.detail: This is uncommon after haemorrhoid surgery and is usually temporary if it occurs. It is more likely in people who already have some weakness of the anal muscles. Tell your surgeon if it happens.

risks.name: The haemorrhoids can come back
risks.detail: Treatment does not always prevent haemorrhoids returning. Keeping stools soft, avoiding straining and keeping fibre and fluids up reduces the chance of recurrence.

risks.name: Difficulty passing urine
risks.detail: This can happen in the first day after anorectal surgery. If you cannot pass urine, contact your surgeon or go to an emergency department, because the bladder can be damaged if it is left too full.

questions.q: Can I avoid surgery?
questions.a: Often, yes. Increasing fibre and fluids, avoiding straining, and treatments such as rubber band ligation help most people. Surgery is only for a minority whose symptoms continue or are severe.

questions.q: How painful is it?
questions.a: It is generally painful for one to two weeks, and excisional surgery is the most painful option. You will be given pain relief and stool softeners, and warm sitz baths help. It gradually improves.

questions.q: What about the first bowel movement?
questions.a: It is often less painful than people fear. Keep your stool soft with fibre, fluids and softeners, and do not put it off. Contact your surgeon if you cannot go at all.

questions.q: How long off work?
questions.a: Many people need one to three weeks away from work, depending on the operation and their job. Your surgeon will advise you.

questions.q: Will they come back?
questions.a: They can. Surgery does not change the underlying tendency. Keeping stools soft, drinking enough fluid and avoiding straining gives you the best chance of staying comfortable.

questions.q: What can I do to prevent another problem?
questions.a: Eat plenty of fibre, drink enough water, avoid straining and long periods on the toilet, and treat constipation early. This advice applies even after successful surgery.

procedures.title: Surgery for anal fissure
procedures.summary: An anal fissure is a painful tear in the lining of the anal canal. Most heal with simple treatment, but long-standing fissures may need a small operation.

sections.heading: What an anal fissure is
body: An anal fissure is a small tear in the skin that lines the anal canal. It most often happens after passing a hard, dry stool, though diarrhoea can also cause one.

The tear causes sharp, severe pain during a bowel movement, and a burning pain that can last for hours afterwards. Many people notice bright red blood on the toilet paper or on the stool. Between bowel movements there is often little or no pain.

The pain causes the anal sphincter muscle to go into spasm. The spasm reduces blood flow to the tear, which slows healing, and the next bowel movement causes more pain. This cycle is why fissures can persist.

Fissures are common. They can occur at any age and in both men and women. A fissure that is not in the midline, or that does not heal, needs further assessment because other conditions can look similar.

sections.heading: Most fissures heal without surgery
body: The majority of anal fissures heal with simple measures. The aim is to soften the stool so it passes easily and to relax the sphincter so blood flow returns and the tear can heal.
Treatment usually includes:
bullets: A high fibre diet, aiming for plenty of fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, with a fibre supplement if needed.
Plenty of fluids, especially water.
Stool softeners if the stool is hard.
Warm shallow baths, called sitz baths, for ten to twenty minutes several times a day, especially after a bowel movement.
A local anaesthetic ointment for pain.
Avoiding strong painkillers containing codeine, because they cause constipation.

sections.heading: Ointments and injections
body: If simple measures are not enough, your doctor may prescribe an ointment that relaxes the internal sphincter muscle. Two common types are glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) ointment and diltiazem ointment. These increase blood flow to the tear and help it heal.

GTN ointment often causes headaches, which can be troublesome. Diltiazem causes headaches less often. Both are usually used for several weeks. Let your doctor know if side effects bother you, as there are alternatives.

Botulinum toxin, sometimes known by the brand name Botox, can be injected into the sphincter muscle to relax it. This is done as a day procedure. It helps a good proportion of people, but the effect wears off after a few months and the fissure can return. It is often used when ointments have not worked, or when there is a concern about continence.

sections.heading: Lateral internal sphincterotomy
body: If a fissure has become chronic and has not healed with other treatment, an operation called a lateral internal sphincterotomy may be recommended. A chronic fissure is one that has been present for roughly eight to twelve weeks or longer, often with a sentinel skin tag or thickened edges.

In this operation, the surgeon makes a small cut in part of the internal anal sphincter muscle. This reduces the resting tension of the muscle, which improves blood flow to the fissure and allows it to heal. Only a small, controlled amount of the muscle is divided.

It is done under a general anaesthetic or sometimes a spinal anaesthetic, usually as a day procedure. Healing rates are high, and most people get good pain relief. Complete healing can still take several weeks.

Because the sphincter muscle is involved in continence, there is a small risk of difficulty controlling wind or stool afterwards. This is uncommon, and when it does occur it is often mild and may settle over time. The risk is higher in women who have had an obstetric injury during childbirth, in people who have had previous anal surgery, and in people with frequent loose stools or diarrhoea. Your surgeon will assess these factors carefully with you before recommending the operation.

An alternative for some people is an advancement flap, where healthy tissue is moved to cover the fissure. This avoids dividing the sphincter muscle and may be preferred when there is a higher risk to continence. It is a more specialised operation and not suitable for everyone.

sections.heading: Recovery
body: Acute pain often improves within a few days of surgery, though complete healing of the fissure can take up to six to twelve weeks. Most people can return to work and daily activities within a few days.

Continue the fibre, fluids and stool softeners afterwards. Even when the pain and bleeding have gone, good bowel habits protect against the fissure coming back. Fissures can recur, particularly after a hard bowel movement.
Contact your surgeon if the pain is not improving, if bleeding becomes heavy, or if you have any trouble controlling wind or stool.

expect: Most heal without surgery
Soft stools and sitz baths first
Surgery is a small day procedure
Healing can take up to 6 to 12 weeks
Small risk to continence, discussed openly

risks.name: Difficulty controlling wind or stool
risks.detail: Lateral internal sphincterotomy carries a small risk of changed continence. It is uncommon and often mild, but it can be persistent. The risk is higher in women with previous childbirth injury, people with prior anal surgery, and people with diarrhoea. Your surgeon will discuss this carefully with you.

risks.name: Bleeding
risks.detail: Some bleeding or spotting is common after the operation. Heavy or non-stop bleeding needs urgent medical attention.

risks.name: Infection
risks.detail: Infection at the operation site is uncommon. It is usually treated with antibiotics and wound care.

risks.name: The fissure may not heal or may return
risks.detail: Most fissures heal after surgery, but some do not, and fissures can recur after a hard bowel movement. Continuing good bowel habits helps reduce this.

risks.name: Headache and low blood pressure from ointments
risks.detail: GTN ointment commonly causes headaches and can lower blood pressure. Diltiazem causes headaches less often. These effects are from the ointment rather than surgery, and usually settle when treatment stops.

risks.name: Difficulty passing urine
risks.detail: This can happen in the first day after anal surgery. If you cannot pass urine, contact your surgeon or attend an emergency department.

questions.q: Will the fissure heal on its own?
questions.a: Most do, with fibre, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths and sometimes a prescribed ointment. Chronic fissures that have been present for many weeks are less likely to heal without further treatment.

questions.q: Will surgery affect my ability to control my bowels?
questions.a: There is a small risk with sphincterotomy, and it is important to discuss it. It is uncommon and often mild, but the risk is higher for some people, including women who have had a childbirth injury. Your surgeon will consider this with you and may recommend an alternative.

questions.q: What are the alternatives to surgery?
questions.a: Ointments such as GTN or diltiazem, and botulinum toxin injections, are used before surgery in most cases. An advancement flap is another surgical option for some people.

questions.q: How long until I feel better?
questions.a: Pain often improves within a few days, but the fissure itself can take six to twelve weeks to heal fully. Keep up the fibre and fluids during that time.

questions.q: Can fissures turn into cancer?
questions.a: No, a fissure does not turn into cancer. However, bleeding and pain from the bottom should always be checked, because other conditions can cause similar symptoms.

questions.q: What if it comes back?
questions.a: Fissures can recur, especially after a hard bowel movement. Continuing good bowel habits helps. If it returns without an obvious cause, further assessment may be needed.

procedures.title: Surgery for anal fistula
procedures.summary: An anal fistula is a small tunnel between the anal canal and the skin near the anus. It usually follows an abscess and almost always needs an operation to cure it.

sections.heading: What an anal fistula is
body: An anal fistula is an abnormal tunnel that runs from the inside of the anal canal to the skin near the anus. It usually forms after an anal abscess, which is an infected cavity filled with pus near the anus or rectum.

Most abscesses start with an infection in one of the small glands inside the anal canal. When the abscess is drained, the channel between the gland and the skin can persist as a fistula. Sometimes the external opening heals over, and the infection builds up again, causing a recurring cycle of pain, swelling and discharge.
Symptoms include discharge of pus or blood, irritation and soreness of the skin around the anus, pain, and sometimes fever. The discharge may come and go if the opening closes and reopens.

sections.heading: Why it needs surgery
body: Fistulae rarely heal on their own. Antibiotics alone do not cure a fistula, although they may be used to settle infection. Without treatment, many people have repeated cycles of abscess and discharge.

The aim of surgery is to close or remove the tunnel while protecting the sphincter muscles that control continence as much as possible. Balancing these two goals is the central challenge of fistula surgery, especially for complex fistulae.

sections.heading: Mapping the fistula first
body: Before planning an operation, the surgeon needs to know exactly where the tunnel runs and how much sphincter muscle it involves. This is called mapping.
Mapping may include:
bullets: An examination under anaesthetic, where the surgeon examines the tract while you are asleep, so you feel no pain.
An MRI scan of the pelvis, which shows the tract and any hidden collections of pus, and is particularly useful for complex or recurrent fistulae.
An endoanal ultrasound, where a small probe is used to image the anal sphincter muscles and the tract.
Sometimes a dye study or examination with a fine probe.

sections.heading: The Goodsall rule
body: The Goodsall rule is an older guide that links the position of the external opening with the likely path of the tunnel, based on where the opening sits in relation to the anus. Openings at the back tend to run in a curved path, while openings at the front tend to run more directly to the anal canal.

It is a rough guide only, and it is not always accurate, especially for openings far from the anus. Modern surgeons rely more on careful examination under anaesthetic, MRI and ultrasound than on the rule alone.

sections.heading: Surgical options
body: There are several operations, and the best one depends on how much sphincter muscle the fistula passes through, whether there has been previous surgery, and whether you have Crohn disease.

Fistulotomy is the division of the tunnel so it heals as an open groove from the inside out. It is the most effective operation for simple, low fistulae that pass through little muscle. Cure rates are high. It is not suitable when a lot of sphincter muscle is involved, because dividing too much muscle risks incontinence.

A seton is a thin piece of rubber or suture threaded through the tunnel and left in place, sometimes for weeks or months. It keeps the tract draining and allows inflammation to settle, and helps the tract mature into firm scar tissue. A definitive repair can then be planned as a second, staged operation. A seton does not usually prevent you from having normal bowel movements.

The LIFT procedure, short for ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract, divides the tunnel in the space between the internal and external sphincter muscles. It avoids cutting the sphincter muscle itself. Success rates are similar to an advancement flap.

An advancement flap is used for complex fistulae or when there is a higher risk of incontinence. The internal opening is covered with a flap of healthy tissue. It does not divide the sphincter, but it is a more demanding operation and the fistula can recur. Mild to moderate continence changes have still been reported after it.
Other options exist, including plugs and glues, and newer techniques continue to be developed. Results vary, and your surgeon will explain what is suitable for you.

sections.heading: The two competing risks
body: The main trade-off in fistula surgery is between the fistula coming back and the risk to continence. Dividing more muscle improves the chance of curing the fistula but increases the risk of difficulty controlling wind or stool. Dividing less muscle protects continence but increases the chance the fistula returns.

For simple, low fistulae the balance usually favours division, with a high cure rate and a low risk to continence. For high or complex fistulae that pass through a lot of muscle, the balance shifts to sphincter-preserving operations, accepting a higher chance of recurrence.
This is why the same fistula may be treated differently in different people. Your surgeon will weigh up the anatomy, your bowel habit, any previous surgery and your own priorities.
A fistula can recur even after successful treatment. If symptoms come back, further assessment and sometimes another operation is needed.

sections.heading: Fistulae and Crohn disease
body: Fistulae are common in people with Crohn disease. They can be more complex, may have multiple tracts, and tend to recur. Repeated operations on the sphincter increase the risk to continence over time.

For this reason, the main treatment for Crohn's-related perianal fistulae is usually medical, with medicines that control the inflammation. Surgery is used mainly to drain infection and sometimes to help the medical treatment work. Treatment is tailored to the individual, and a team approach with a gastroenterologist is common.
If you have Crohn disease, tell your surgeon, because it changes the plan.

sections.heading: Recovery
body: Most fistula operations are done as day surgery, though some people stay overnight. Pain is managed with tablets, fibre and fluids. Warm sitz baths help, and it is important to avoid constipation, especially if you are taking painkillers that slow the bowel.

How long you need away from work depends on the operation and your job. Ask your surgeon to plan this with you before the operation. If you have a seton in place, you can usually carry on with normal bowel function while it is there.

Often day surgery
Seton may be used as a first stage
Recurrence and continence are the trade-off

risks.name: The fistula returning
risks.detail: Fistulae can recur even after successful surgery, and recurrence rates differ between operations. Sphincter-preserving repairs tend to have a higher chance of recurrence than a fistulotomy for a simple low fistula.

risks.name: Difficulty controlling wind or stool
risks.detail: This is the main risk of operations that divide sphincter muscle, and it increases with the amount of muscle involved and with repeated surgery. Sphincter-preserving operations reduce but do not completely remove this risk. Your surgeon will discuss it with you in detail.

risks.name: Bleeding
risks.detail: Some bleeding is common after fistula surgery. Heavy or non-stop bleeding needs urgent medical attention.

risks.name: Infection or delayed healing
risks.detail: The wound can become infected or heal slowly, particularly with complex fistulae or Crohn disease. This may need dressing care, antibiotics or further surgery.

risks.name: Seton-related symptoms
risks.detail: A seton can cause some discharge, irritation or discomfort while it is in place. It is usually well tolerated and normal bowel function continues.

risks.name: Difficulty passing urine
risks.detail: This can happen in the first day after anal surgery. If you cannot pass urine, contact your surgeon or attend an emergency department.

questions.q: Can the fistula heal without surgery?
questions.a: It is uncommon. Antibiotics may settle infection, but the tunnel itself rarely closes permanently without an operation.

questions.q: Why do I need an MRI?
questions.a: An MRI shows where the tunnel runs and whether there are hidden collections of pus. This helps your surgeon plan the safest operation and decide how much muscle is involved.

questions.q: What is a seton?
questions.a: A seton is a thin loop of rubber or suture threaded through the tunnel to keep it draining and let inflammation settle. It may stay in for weeks or months before a definitive repair is done.

questions.q: Will I be incontinent after surgery?
questions.a: Any operation that divides sphincter muscle carries some risk. Your surgeon will choose the operation that best balances curing the fistula against protecting your continence, and will explain the risks for your particular fistula.

questions.q: What if I have Crohn disease?
questions.a: Crohn's-related fistulae are usually treated mainly with medicines, with surgery used to control infection and support the medical treatment. Tell your surgeon so the plan can be tailored.

questions.q: How long will I need off work?
questions.a: This depends on the operation and your job. Some people return within a week or two, others need longer. Ask your surgeon to plan this with you beforehand.
